title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, authorities say
description: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local aut
body: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

schema.headline: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, authorities say

title: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
description: Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going in
body: Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín, paving the way for their return to Spain.Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party.He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him.Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained.While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021.Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions.In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad."My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said.It is still not known when he might return to Spain.Comín, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP.The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco.The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election.But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda.The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election.But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters.And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time.

schema.headline: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules

title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
description: As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory fe
body: As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.He was briefed by federal police – whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year."We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds."We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life."This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia."Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people."They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night."Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said."I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that's an important part of our democracy."

schema.headline: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car

title: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
description: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donal
body: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump."The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship. "Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote."If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her -  or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated."Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC. "The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe." Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation". But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago. Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

schema.headline: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'

title: Alberta heads to polls to decide whether to hold vote on separation from Canada
description: People in the province of Alberta head to the polls on Monday to decide whether to hold a binding referendum at a later date on separating from Canada
body: People in the province of Alberta head to the polls on Monday to decide whether to hold a binding referendum at a later date on separating from Canada. The vote was called earlier this year by the leader of the province, Danielle Smith, after a grassroots group gathered about 300,000 signatures on a petition that asked for a binding referendum on separation.Many of those who support separation say the oil-rich province's economic growth has been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa.But those who want Alberta to remain part of Canada - who include Prime Minister Mark Carney - have called for the country to show unity in the face of external pressures.Polls have suggested that the majority of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, though the pre-vote debate alone has proven divisive. Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people. The province's population is about five million people.If Albertans do vote on Monday to move ahead with a binding referendum, that could happen as soon as 2027, Smith has said. Smith's decision to allow Monday's vote came in spite of the fact that a court blocked the pro-separation petition, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated from Canada.Following the judge's ruling, First Nations groups have branded Smith's decision to allow the voting process to play out as "undemocratic" and "authoritarian".Smith, the leader of the United Conservative Party of Alberta (UCP), has defended her decision to put the issue to voters. She opposes separation herself, but says the process gives the province's residents a chance to have their say on the issue.The key question on the voting paper will ask: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"The separatist movement is led by Mitch Sylvestre, a gun shop owner from the town of Bonnyville, and Jeffrey Rath, a lawyer based in Calgary. They are both members of a group called the Alberta Prosperity Project, which argues that the province's economic growth has been hindered by years of Liberal party rule in Ottawa.Successive Liberal governments of the last 10 years have put environmental policies above helping Alberta develop its oil and gas sector, they argue. They say Alberta would get to keep more of its wealth if it splits from Canada.Chris Scott, founder of pro-separatist group Let's Talk Alberta, told BBC News on the eve of the poll that the campaign had already achieved some of its goals, regardless of what happened on Monday. "The key is the conversation has started and it needs to continue," he said. "What's started can't be stopped now," he added.Those who oppose separation say a newly independent Alberta would be left responsible for billions of dollars in debt. They warn that the uncertainty - which they liken to the UK's Brexit vote to leave the European Union in 2016 - would drive thousands of jobs and investment out of the province.Pro-independence voters told the BBC in Edmonton over the weekend that they feel their voice is not heard in Ottawa, the national capital. "We really need to send a message to Ottawa, " said Jennifer Trudeau, who calls herself a sovereigntist. She said she did not want a full divorce from Canada, but believes the province needs to "assert its rights". At a separate unity rally in Edmonton, people told the BBC that they were proud Albertans but felt it was better to keep the country together. "Alberta is a strong province, but it is important that it stays within a united Canada," said Michele Jackson. "That is critical to me. I am Canadian 100%." Micah Sellers called the question about whether the province should pursue independence "ridiculous". "It's a waste of money," he said. "It's a distraction from real issues in Alberta and in Canada. I think if we're going to be asked, everyone should vote to remain." Carney has called on voters to deliver a decisive vote against separation. Speaking at a rally on Thursday, he warned that the stakes were high. "The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," Carney said, echoing warnings he has made in the past about his country's ongoing trade war with the United States.Alongside the separation question, Albertans will vote on nine other issues - a number of which focus on whether the province should have more control over its immigration system.Hundreds of thousands of people had voted early by post ahead of Monday, and early figures suggested a strong voter turnout. The province's election officials will count the ballots by hand, and have 48 hours to complete the task - starting from no earlier than 20:00 local time on Monday (02:00 GMT on Tuesday).The key question, on separation, will be counted in its entirety first. Officials have said results should be available in the early hours of Tuesday.

schema.headline: Alberta heads to polls to decide whether to hold vote on separation from Canada

title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
description: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table."I am in the
body: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table."I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence.

schema.headline: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going

title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
description: Figure caption, The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raidBy Quentin SommervilleInternational
body: Figure caption, The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raidBy Quentin SommervilleInternational correspondent, Columbus, OhioWarning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicideThe few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood."This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars."You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune.We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape. Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.America's War on Drugs: The Synthetic WaveExtraordinary access shows how strong synthetic drugs are changing America's drug crisis.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," says Mike as he lights up a few grains of fentanylImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Mike, a former army veteran, acts as our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States.At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over.It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl.The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added.When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce."Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me.They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat.Recovery group offering hopeAt the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma.They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty.One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life.As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid."It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting at Glenwood ChurchImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, One of those gathered at the church, Tonya, recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same timeBoth in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose"."In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers.Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so."The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it."Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Scott Sanders, 65, is almost 10 years sober and runs Hope DealersOverdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds.His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina.That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine."The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements."And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois.Watch the documentary on YouTube, externalI meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity.Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means.He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever.When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico. "If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability."And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear.  "Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me.A novel approach Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening."In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel."The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures.Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens.It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters."Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained.Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, In Chicago's largest jail, drugs were soaked in the pages of books and in lettersIn August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search.As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of.As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates.The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper.Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters that enter the jail test positive for moistureOutside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them.In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell.Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs.She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing."Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants.The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous"."Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Karen, a recovery worker, tends to a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair in an upscale part of town Dart has been sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs was progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me. And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics."The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it."Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail. "You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way."'A lot of people are struggling'Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track.It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Karen says her pregnancy was an opportunity to get clean. She's 17 years free from hard drugs As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed."A pregnancy test changed her mind. She then spent time in Cook County jail for theft. Her parents, sensing an opportunity for her to get clean, refused to pay her bail money. So Karen got clean and Abby was born inside the jail.When I ask Abby, who wants to become a tattoo artist, whether she's ever been tempted to experiment with drugs, she says: "Nah, I've seen it mess with my family too much, with my dad, my mum, killing my aunt, my uncles. You know, it's not worth it to get high for like a couple of hours."She continues: "There's a lot of people are struggling, especially that our country is raising our prices, raising the prices on food and it's causing it. A lot of mental health now is very expensive so people can't get help, and one way they can turn to that is by drugs."Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis, but it is never the same crisis. It has shifted from heroin, to prescription opioids to fentanyl and now to a whole new range of synthetics.Successive administrations have fought - and lost - the war against drugs. The dealers, the suppliers, the cartels and users all adapt, always a few steps ahead of efforts to stop them.Additional reporting by Darren ConwayIf you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

schema.headline: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis

title: Italy plans tougher security measures after violent Milan protests
description: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is poised to approve emergency security measures, according to local media, after protests over rising costs bro
body: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is poised to approve emergency security measures, according to local media, after protests over rising costs broke out into violent clashes in Milan.The measures include extending preventative detention to minors and restricting group gatherings, Milanese paper Corriere della Sera reported.Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers over the weekend. More than 250 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Italian police said.The expected crackdown comes after Meloni chaired an emergency security meeting on Monday afternoon. No official announcements have been made.More than 5,000 people gathered in Milan over the weekend. As well as clashes between police and some protesters, stores were looted and property was set on fire.High-end shops in the city's centre closed early on Monday, with many boarding up their windows over fears of further damage. Measures to crack down on youth gangs are expected to be approved as early as Tuesday as part of a decree law, according to Corriere della Sera.Local media reports suggest social media was used to invite young people to Italy's squares over the weekend.Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania, in recent weeks.Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried this represented a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself".Speaking to Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world".Of the 271 people taken to police stations on Sunday, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured. Violence between protesters and police also spread to other cities in the north.Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder."To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos".The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting."Do not be ambiguous about this," she said in a post on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification".Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported.The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets.

schema.headline: Italy plans tougher security measures after violent Milan protests

title: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda
description: A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.Robert K
body: A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend. The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety."It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics."Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

schema.headline: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda

title: Lula and Bolsonaro trade barbs in Brazil election debate
description: Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week be
body: Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week before the run-off presidential election.Polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck and the televised debate was  hailed as a chance for both to sway undecided voters. But the showdown was marked by personal attacks and analysts have warned that its aggressive tone may increase the abstention rate further.In the first round of voting, held on 4 October, Bolsonaro defied opinion polls by securing a narrow lead over Lula. Sunday's debate was the first of two before the vote. The second is planned for Friday, just two days before polls open.Flávio Bolsonaro is standing for the Liberal Party after his father, Jair Bolsonaro - who governed from 2018 to 2022 - was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison for plotting to overthrow Lula after the latter beat him in the 2022 election. The younger Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula's 45.2%, with both falling short of the 50% of the valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round. Since the return to democracy in 1988, there has been no instance in which the candidate who lost in the first round went on to win in the second but Lula has told his supporters that he will "win in extra time". Analysts consulted by BBC News Brasil were struck by how much the debate was dominated not by issues but personal attacks.Yuri Sanches from pollsters AtlasIntel said it was a debate in which no policies were discussed and there were no rational arguments. "The independent voter, who is sometimes against Bolsonaro and sometimes against the Workers' Party [of Lula], came out of it with a very negative impression."Lucas Aragão from political analysis firm Arko Advice said Bolsonaro had appeared calmer during the debate and seemed to have managed to "get under Lula's skin". Rafael Cortez from consulting firm da Tendências Consultoria, however, argued that Lula had managed to score a goal when he said he would open up his financial and phone records and those of his family to judicial scrutiny, and challenged his rival to do the same before Sunday's run-off.Many observers criticised the format of the debate, which was described as chaotic at times, with each of the candidates pacing around the TV studio as the other was speaking.One heated exchange saw Bolsonaro telling Lula he should come stand next to him so that the two could talk.Referring to alleged links between the senator and paramilitary vigilante groups, Lula said "I don't want to be close to you", and that he wanted to maintain "distance from the Bolsonaro family" and "the militia". Bolsonaro, who has dismissed the allegations as fake news, in turn tried to bait Lula by saying, "On second thoughts, maybe it's better to keep my distance so that my wallet isn't stolen."He also accused the Workers' Party of being corrupt, holding up the palm of his hand on which he had scribbled "CORRUPTO" (Portuguese for "corrupt)."Take a piece of paper and a pen and jot down 'corrupt' and you'll see that it has two letters in the middle here together," he said, pointing to PT, the initials of the Workers' Party in Portuguese. Bolsonaro, who is campaigning on a iron-fist approach to crime, challenged Lula to explain why crime rates had gone up during his four years in power. He also alleged, without providing any evidence, that "the majority of convicts vote for Lula".Lula shot back with a thinly veiled reference to Flávio's convicted father, Jair, saying; "I wish it was 100%, even your father".

schema.headline: Lula and Bolsonaro trade barbs in Brazil election debate

title: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'
description: The fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.It br
body: The fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.It broke out in a grassy training area at a base in the province of Alberta and spread rapidly due to strong winds."The fire was 1km (0.6 miles) away when the wind shifted," said Maj-Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division of the Canadian Armed Forces. "It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds."Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". Officials have ruled out the possibility of "any terrorist activity".The blaze began at about 16:00 (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases. The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.Of the 39 injured people receiving care in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.In account of Saturday's events, Rutland told reporters that members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range.He told reporters that officials knew about the fire on the base for several hours, but it was decided that training "could carry on for a certain amount of time"."I spoke to my commander last night, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them," Rutland said.Rutland said it was not yet known what exactly caused the fire.Some witnesses had said they had heard explosions, fuelling speculation that oil and gas infrastructure may have been hit and sparked the fire. But Rutland said authorities "do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure".The Canadian Armed Forces has said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". Forecasters had issued a wind warning on Saturday for large parts of Alberta, predicting wind gusts of up to 90km/h (66mph), Canadian broadcaster CBS said.According to Rutland, the investigation may take at least a month.Wainwright, about 130 miles east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.

schema.headline: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'

title: Tiger Shroff: Bollywood actor survives shooting attempt in Mumbai
description: Police in India's Mumbai city are investigating a shooting attempt on Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, who survived without sustaining any gunshot wounds
body: Police in India's Mumbai city are investigating a shooting attempt on Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, who survived without sustaining any gunshot wounds.The 36-year-old was shot at on Sunday evening while he was in a car leaving a football ground in Juhu suburb. Videos showed at least two men firing multiple shots at close range at the front passenger seat of Shroff's car while it was moving slowly past a crowd.Two people, including Shroff's driver, were injured, according to the police. Three people were detained in Rajasthan on Monday in connection with the incident, the police said. The attack has sent shockwaves through Bollywood, with celebrities raising concerns about Shroff's safety. Several actors and political figures in Mumbai have been targeted by gunmen in recent years.Shroff, the son of veteran Bollywood actor Jackie Shroff, made his film debut with Heropanti in 2014. He has appeared in many action films, and is popular with fans for his dancing and martial arts skills.He is also a professional footballer and made his debut for Mumbay FC in October 2024 in a regional tournament. He was leaving the football ground after his regular practice session when the attack happenedEknath Shinde, deputy chief minister of Maharashtra state of which Mumbai is the capital, visited Shroff after the shooting on Sunday evening, and said the actor had been left "shaken" by the attack."These attempts to intimidate people will not be tolerated, and we will put an end to this hooliganism," Shinde said.In a photograph showing Shroff with Shinde, the actor is seen shirtless with some bandages on his upper body. It's not clear yet what injuries he sustained.Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis described the incident as "serious and condemnable", and said that the police would arrest some people "very soon".He said he had told Shroff that he should not worry, and that the government would ensure his "complete safety".Rajasthan police said two of the three suspects detained were from the northern states of Haryana and Bihar and had been living in Mumbai for the past few years. The third suspect is a minor.They are expected to be handed over to Mumbai Police later in the day.The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA), a large union, condemned the attack, alleging that gangsters were deliberately targeting people in the film industry to create an "atmosphere of fear" and extort money from celebrities.In a statement, the association criticised the government and police for failing to prevent such attacks. It called for strict action against those responsible and better security for film industry workers and their families.The association also said the incident was a reminder of the 1990s, when criminal gangs wielded considerable influence in the city. It said that the film industry should not have to "work under the shadow of fear".Police have not yet confirmed who was behind the shooting. But Indian media reports have been widely reporting that an audio clip has surfaced in which a man claiming to be linked to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang says he is responsible.Bishnoi is currently lodged in a high-security prison in Gujarat state in connection with several high-profile cases.The authenticity of the recording and the man's claims have not been independently verified and police have not confirmed the gang's involvement yet.But the reports have brought the Bishnoi gang back into the headlines.In 2024, police arrested two people allegedly linked to the Bishnoi gang for a gun attack that targeted the home of Bollywood superstar Salman Khan.That same year, influential Indian politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Mumbai. His murder, in a bustling neighbourhood in Mumbai, was also reportedly linked to people associated with the Bishnoi gang.Additional reporting by BBC Marathi

schema.headline: Tiger Shroff: Bollywood actor survives shooting attempt in Mumbai

title: Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack
description: Australian MP Helen Haines is critically ill in hospital in Melbourne after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says may have b
body: Australian MP Helen Haines is critically ill in hospital in Melbourne after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says may have been a deliberate attack. The independent MP, 65, was struck outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, in the state of Victoria, on Monday afternoon.A man, 43, from the nearby town of Tarrawingee was detained at the scene by a passerby and police say a knife was found in the car.Police are investigating whether it was an "intentional act" but say they do not believe there is an "ongoing threat to the community".Political leaders have expressed shock and dismay, with Albanese saying "there is no place for violence in a democracy".   While Albanese said it was too early to understand the motive behind what had happened, he did say the political temperature had been rising in Australia. His Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke backed up that statement with figures showing that reports of threatening or harassing behaviour towards politicians had risen from 951 to 1,067 in the past year.Haines was hit by a white Toyota Landcruiser at 15:35 (04:35 GMT) outside her office on Murphy Street in Wangaratta, police say.The town, which has a population of around 30,000, is a few hours north-east of Melbourne.A witness told Australian broadcaster ABC they had heard a bang and seen a woman pinned between two cars, external.Haines was initially taken to a hospital in Wangaratta but later moved to Melbourne by helicopter.After being subdued and detained by the passersby, the suspect was arrested by police. Announcing that counter terror police were involved in the investigation, the prime minister said: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."In a statement, Victoria Police said: "At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act."It is not known yet if the parties are known to each other... The investigation remains ongoing."Although not necessarily a household name across Australia, in the political sphere Helen Haines is both well-known and well regarded as an anti-corruption campaigner.There has been an outpouring of messages from politicians and party leaders across the breadth of the political spectrum. In an age of increasingly divisive politics, she is seen by many as a unifying force.The independent MP has only been a federal parliamentarian for a relatively short time, having been elected in 2019. However, in that time she has become an influential advocate for integrity in politics.Haines proposed legislation for a national anti-corruption watchdog in 2021, and has been credited for driving the creation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission under Labor in the previous parliamentary term.She currently sits on the parliamentary committee responsible for its oversight.Haines has often banded together with other key independents on issues that include climate action and gender equality.Allegra Spender, another independent MP who has collaborated with Haines, called her "the best of us".

schema.headline: Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack

title: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya
description: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.Mackenzie ordered me
body: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows". Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings". Those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus", the judge said.One witness stated that a pregnant woman had been barred from nursing her new-born baby, who died 12 days later. "She was instructed to fast to death and follow her children," the witness said.Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children. But this is the first time the pastor has faced a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.He was arrested in 2023, after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie had led his followers from across the country.Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie."I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC from his home in the coastal town of Malindi, 70km (43 miles) from Shakahola."All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said ahead of the verdict, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day."Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old.""We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another." Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town. "We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside."The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him. Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him". When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned."My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said.The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said.By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers.Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest. He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover."My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said."I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest."Many of the bodies are still unidentified owing to their advanced state of decomposition. In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me". "Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said before the verdict was announced."I still love him and he is still my pastor."In contrast Dan Mackenzie believed his father should be found guilty of murder."He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing," also speaking before the verdict.

schema.headline: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya

title: World Food Programme forced to cut aid to Gaza due to funding shortages
description: Image caption, Dalal al-Dahdouh said the WFP food handouts her family received were insufficient even before the cutsByYolande KnellMiddle East corres
body: Image caption, Dalal al-Dahdouh said the WFP food handouts her family received were insufficient even before the cutsByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalemOne of the main suppliers of food aid to the Gaza Strip, the World Food Programme (WFP), says that it is being forced to "drastically reduce lifesaving assistance" to the Palestinian territory due to funding shortages.Overall, the number of people helped by the UN agency will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. The cuts will hit as winter approaches and at a time when many families in Gaza are still struggling to feed themselves.One effect is that the number of hot meals that are currently being provided by community kitchens will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day.Families living in hard-to-reach areas, for example near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates Israel's area of military control, will receive a meal every other day instead of daily.Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population remains displaced and two-thirds rely on food aid to survive.Image caption, Mervat al-Satari, a mother-of-five, says the cuts are a "disaster""It's a disaster! What will we do with these reduced rations? How will we provide for the little ones?" said Mervat al-Satari, a displaced Palestinian mother-of-five at a camp in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis after being told of the WFP's news. "Sometimes we wait for these meals to eat.""This will affect us a lot. The daily aid was somehow ticking the box but now it will be every two days," said Sawsan Bahloul, who is also from al-Mawasi and is a mother of three. She added that the portions given by the community kitchen - usually pasta or lentils with occasional potatoes and aubergines - were already too small to feed her family.The Palestine director for the WFP, Shaun Hughes, is clear that the cuts are being made because of finances, and "not because the needs are coming down, or because we don't have access - we do."Image caption, Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million people are displaced, with many living in camps like those in al-MawasiAlready, since July, there have been reductions in cash transfers provided to some half a million people, meaning they have less money to buy food in local markets. The number of Gazans given bags of flour and ration boxes by the WFP will now fall from 1.1 million to 600,000 each month.The WFP received less than half as much funding for its Palestinian operations in 2026 as in previous years. The agency says it urgently needs $450m (£338m) to maintain "critical" operations over the next six months.Despite a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel that was agreed a year ago, violence has continued, including almost daily Israeli strikes, and humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire.There has been no reconstruction and little recovery, with Israel tightly controlling the entry of goods through crossings. While food markets are now well stocked, few can afford to buy from them. More than 80% of people in Gaza are unemployed so most of the population relies on aid.Image caption, Two-thirds of the population relies on food aid to survive, according to UN-backed expertsFamilies currently receiving the WFP food handouts complained to the BBC that already these were insufficient and gave them little diversity in their diets."The flour isn't enough and the food boxes aren't enough either," said Dalal al-Dahdouh, who is living in the ruins of her home in Gaza City with her family of eight. She fears the new cuts will have "a major impact".The mother draws a contrast between the current desperate situation and life before the war. "In the past, thank God, we had our own home and a wonderful life. We had fresh vegetables, proper sanitation facilities and our own land," she said. "Now we live entirely on aid, including WFP vouchers."There is no cooking gas available in Gaza because the Israeli government considers it a "dual use" item that could be used by Hamas for military purposes. Wood is expensive, so many families send their children into the street to find plastic and cardboard to burn as fuel to make bread or heat food."It's still a very concerning humanitarian situation, people living in brutal conditions, most people still without a proper home, living in tents, poor access to water and sanitation and healthcare," Hughes of the WFP told the BBC. "Cuts to food assistance are going to compound that hardship that families have been facing for three years now."Image caption, Families, including Sawsan Bahloul's, are forced to burn plastic and cardboard as fuel for cookingHumanitarian workers say that despite a modest improvement in Gaza compared to a year ago, acute food insecurity and the risk of famine returning continue to loom over the territory.In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) - the world's foremost experts on food security - reported that two-thirds of the population - 1.4 million people - were "expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026".For now, the WFP says it can continue supporting bakeries that provide one-third of Gaza's bread needs and provide nutritional assistance to about 300,000 women and children. It also delivers health food snacks to some 200,000 children.In the occupied West Bank, the WFP is continuing to give assistance to some 200,000 Palestinians, having halved the number of recipients in September. The agency says food insecurity is rising in the territory mostly due to increased Israeli settler violence and Palestinian displacement.

schema.headline: World Food Programme forced to cut aid to Gaza due to funding shortages
